description: The humans of the medieval past lived in societies as complex as ours. What guidelines can we glean about modern life and how best to live it from history? From codes of honor for warriors and leaders to advice for domestic life and gender relations, Hávamál (The Sayings of the High One) contains fragments of wisdom inherited from the Viking age of Nordic history. Pairing the adages found in this poem of Viking etiquette with Enlightenment ethical reasoning will give students a comparative look at how ethical systems shape and are shaped by history and society. Students will then explore ethical reasoning in literature from the golden age of the Icelandic Commonwealth. Through a close reading of Njal's Saga students will explore the nexus of power, law, and ethics. Comparing Njal's family's uses and abuses of law and power to contemporary issues will allow students to critically evaluate their own positionality and ethics. Finally, a reading of the kingly saga of St. Olaf alongside Kit Christensen's work on justice and revenge will conclude the course and give students greater knowledge of their institution's namesake. Ultimately students will work to develop a tool set for how to critically assess ethical reasoning presented to them by historical sources and how to productively engage with the lessons of the past both historic and personal.
name: Top: Viking Ethics
title: Transdisciplinary Topics in Nordic Studies
